response.strategies:
Mostly random! I noticed that if the differences are only texture-- that would be the easiest.
Sometimes gave up and reset when got stuck trying to transform a shape/shade into a shape/shade that I was missing.
response.achievement_strategies: Not sure if there was a real strategy but I tried to either get the shape/shade to the right ones; textures were the easiest one to change/match to the goal (so that was a secondary priority).
response.instruction_feedback:
I think I didn't quite understand what the "high", "medium", and "low" shade referred to. But then I realized it meant Dark-blue/black; blue; light-blue. On the instructions on the right, I would change the color of the text for "high", "medium", "low" to match the same hexcolor for the shades you are referring to. I think that would make things explicit. Similarly, you could also embed example images for the textures (e.g., plain, dotted, etc.) instead of using the words in the instructions.

I still wasn't too sure if high shade + high shade can ever produce a low shade, or if it always goes to medium shade (similarly for low + low shade, if this can produce a high shade). Basically, is the only way to get to the shade on the other side of the spectrum through medium + medium?
response.improvement: The detailed instructions we saw in the tutorial could have illustrated images and also colored text (when referring to shades)!

stimulus:
Goal Selection Study Debrief

Thank you for your participation in our research study.

Much research shows that goals change how people learn and make decisions. This study examines how people choose their own goals, and then make decisions in order to achieve those goals.

If you are interested in reading some research about this topic, here are two references:

  • Molinaro, G., & Collins, A. G. E. (2023). A goal-centric outlook on learning. Trends in Cognitive Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tics.2023.08.011
  • Chu, J., Tenenbaum, J. B., & Schulz, L. E. (2024). In praise of folly: Flexible goals and human cognition. Trends in Cognitive Sciences, 28(7), 628-642. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tics.2024.03.006

If you have any questions or comments, please do not hesitate to ask us. Thank you for your participation.
